Library of Congress opens experiential gallery for children

By AV Magazine in Government and defence, Systems design and integration, US&Canada, Visitor attractions September 9, 2026 0

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 101:11
Instaread

Creative agency Hyperquake has combined projection mapping, RFID-enabled objects and interactive displays to help young visitors explore the library’s primary sources independently.

The Library of Congress has opened The Source, an experiential research gallery where interactive AV technology helps children explore primary sources independently.

Part of the A Library for You initiative, the 370 sq metre space uses projection-mapped animation, RFID-enabled objects and digital workstations to introduce visitors aged eight to 15 to the library’s vast collections in film, text, sound and image.

Skolnick Architecture led the interpretive planning and exhibition design, appointing Potion (now Hyperquake) to develop the suite of digital interactive installations that structure the research journey.

Media development was initially led by Potion founder Philip R. Tiongson and producer Claire Bradley, whose team now forms the core of Hyperquake’s experiences group, ensuring continuity in the studio’s inclusive, research-driven approach to interactive AV design.

Working closely with Skolnick’s interpretive planners and the library’s content experts, Hyperquake created a sequence of linked physical-digital experiences that guide children through the Library’s research methodology, allowing them to examine real artefacts, uncover context and build confidence as emerging researchers.

The experience begins in the Welcome Room, where a five-sided Card Catalog becomes an AV centrepiece: opening drawers triggers projection-mapped animations that spill across the structure, revealing items from across the collections. Nearby, a Librarian Desk introduces seven staff members on screen, explaining how researchers work with primary sources and directing visitors to four themed Collections Zones.

In the Collections Room, Hyperquake’s digital interactives anchor each zone. More than 200 RFID-enabled objects can be scanned at Investigation Stations, where children zoom into manuscripts, magnify historic images, scrub audio recordings and step through film clips frame by frame on responsive displays. Replica Tools—including a film projector, record player and microfilm reader—provide hands-on encounters with traditional media formats, each offering quick, intuitive interactions that encourage exploration and comparison.

Further along, the Researcher Desk presents curated archival boxes and on-screen narratives showing how real researchers, including young people, have used Library materials to pursue their own questions, reinforcing the AV-led process visitors have just experienced.

The journey culminates at the Source Book, a large-scale interactive installation where visitors use digital tools to create collages and set their own research intentions, which are then added to an ever-changing projection wall that reflects the gallery’s collective inquiry.

“The Source is not an exhibit: it is a centre for active research,” said Mary Franck, creative director of experiences at Hyperquake. “Our goal was to design interactions that feel magical, intuitive and empowering. By augmenting tactile artefacts with digital layers of discovery, we help kids see themselves as researchers from the moment they walk in.”
